item.title: Enrollment protocol
item.description:
The wire contract between the clients and the server. It is defined once in claimward-vpn-client/pkg/protocol (HTTP) and proto/routes/v1/routes.proto (gRPC), and imported by both sides.

Every authenticated request sends the person’s bearer as Authorization: Bearer <token>, never in the body: a GitHub OAuth access token (a github provider), an OIDC ID token (oidc), or a go-authn access token (go-authn). Since server v0.14.0 the request also names the provider that issued it, in the header Claimward-Provider: <id> (gRPC: the metadata claimward-provider), an id from the discovery document’s providers. The token is judged by that provider alone. No header is 401 missing_provider; an id the server does not list, or several ids, is 401 unknown_provider. Request bodies are JSON, at most 64 KiB, and unknown fields are refused.

POST /api/v1/enroll

Request:

{
 "public_key": "<wireguard base64 public key>",
 "device": { "name": "alice-mbp", "os": "darwin", "platform": "app-osx" },
 "tenant": "hpc"
}

tenant is optional: without it the server uses the person’s only tenant. The helpers send os darwin, linux or windows and platform app-osx, app-linux or app-windows.

Response 200:

{
 "assigned_ip": "10.80.0.5/32",
 "server_public_key": "<base64>",
 "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820",
 "allowed_ips": ["10.80.0.0/24"],
 "dns": ["10.80.0.1"],
 "grpc_endpoint": "vpn.example.com:8444",
 "persistent_keepalive": 25,
 "lease_expires_at": "2026-10-06T10:00:00Z"
}

allowed_ips and dns are the tenant’s. dns is left out when the tenant has none, grpc_endpoint when the server advertises no RouteService (GRPC_ENDPOINT). mtu is the tunnel MTU in bytes (an integer, 1280 to 9000), left out when the server has none to advertise. Since server v0.7.0 it is always set: TUNNEL_MTU, or the uplink MTU minus 80 (at most 1420). The client applies it, then lowers it to fit its own path (the interface MTU towards the endpoint minus 60 for IPv4, 80 for IPv6, never below 1280); it never raises it. Absent means 1420.

GET /api/v1/tenants

Response 200: the tenants the caller may connect to.

[ { "id": "default", "name": "Default" } ]

POST /api/v1/heartbeat 

{ "public_key": "<base64>" }

Response 200: { "lease_expires_at": "..." }. 404 not_enrolled if the key is not enrolled by the caller, 403 not_a_member once the person has left the session’s tenant, 403 key_not_registered (go-authn) once the provider no longer lists the key.

POST /api/v1/deregister 

{ "public_key": "<base64>" }

Response 204, also for a key that is not enrolled. 403 not_owner if the key belongs to another person.

GET /healthz

Response 200: { "status": "ok" }, unauthenticated.

GET /.well-known/claimward-configuration

The public discovery document (since server v0.13.0), unauthenticated, so that a client can learn how to sign in before it does. The path follows RFC 8615 section 3; a claim without a value is omitted, as in RFC 8414 section 3.2. Public values only, never a secret. Response 200, application/json, Cache-Control: public, max-age=300; any other method is refused with 405.

{
 "version": 2,
 "server_name": "Lab",
 "providers": [
 { "id": "hub", "kind": "github", "name": "GitHub", "github_client_id": "Iv1.0123456789abcdef" },
 { "id": "campus", "kind": "oidc", "name": "Campus", "oidc_issuer": "https://idp.example.org", "oidc_client_id": "claimward" }
 ],
 "exclusive": false,
 "logo": { "path": "/.well-known/claimward-logo.svg", "sha256": "<hex>" }
}

Version 2 (server v0.14.0, breaking) replaces the single provider and its fields of version 1 by the list providers, one entry per provider of PROVIDERS_FILE, in file order: id (what the client sends in Claimward-Provider), kind (github, oidc or go-authn), name (shown to the person), then github_client_id for github, oidc_issuer and oidc_client_id for oidc and go-authn. A client of version 0.10.0 or later reads it; it refuses a document of a version it does not know. server_name appears only when SERVER_NAME is set, logo only when SERVER_LOGO_FILE is. exclusive is SERVER_EXCLUSIVE: this server refuses to share the machine with other Claimward tunnels, clients refuse to connect it alongside others, and refuse others while it is connected.

GET /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg

The server’s logo (since server v0.14.0), unauthenticated, present only when SERVER_LOGO_FILE is set; otherwise 404. The discovery document’s logo gives its path and the sha256 (hex) of its bytes, so a client can cache it and notice a change. Response 200: Content-Type: image/svg+xml, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox, and ETag set to the same hash; a request with a matching If-None-Match gets 304. The server validates the file at start (at most 64 KiB, no script, no external reference, no DOCTYPE) and refuses to start on an invalid one. A client must still treat it as untrusted and render it as an image, never inline.

Errors

Non-2xx responses carry:

{ "error": "invalid_token", "message": "…" }
Code Status Meaning
missing_token / invalid_token 401 no bearer, or the provider’s verification failed (including an organisation or domain allowlist)
missing_provider 401 no Claimward-Provider header (since v0.14.0)
unknown_provider 401 the header names a provider the server does not list, or several (since v0.14.0)
bad_public_key / bad_request 400 malformed input
key_not_registered 403 go-authn: the key is not registered at the provider by this person
not_a_member 403 the tenant asked for is not one of the caller’s, or no longer is
not_owner 403 deregister: the key belongs to another person
not_enrolled 404 heartbeat: no enrollment of this key by the caller
key_taken 409 enroll: the key is enrolled by another person
tenant_required 409 enroll: the caller belongs to several tenants and named none; the message lists them
pool_exhausted 503 no free address in VPN_CIDR
gateway_error 500 the peer could not be added to WireGuard

RouteService (gRPC) 

package claimward.routes.v1;

service RouteService {
 rpc Watch(WatchRequest) returns (stream RouteUpdate);
}
message WatchRequest { string public_key = 1; }
message RouteUpdate {
 repeated string allowed_ips = 1;
 repeated string dns = 2;
 uint64 serial = 3; // increases on each change
}

The server listens on GRPC_ADDR and advertises GRPC_ENDPOINT in the enrollment response. The bearer travels in the metadata, authorization: Bearer <token>, with the provider in claimward-provider, and is verified as for the HTTP API (UNAUTHENTICATED when either is wrong). Watch sends the current set at once, then a new one each time the tenant’s routes change, for the tenant the device enrolled into, found by public_key, which must be enrolled by the caller (NOT_FOUND otherwise, PERMISSION_DENIED once the person has left that tenant).

The server serves it over TLS with TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY. The clients (pkg/routeclient) speak TLS to it, checked against the system’s roots, except to a loopback address, and refuse a plaintext one.

item.title: Server
item.description:
claimward-vpn-server v0.14.0 is the control plane. It verifies the bearer a device presents, allocates VPN addresses, and programs the WireGuard gateway with one peer per enrolled device. It runs on the gateway host, beside an existing wg0: Linux (nftables) or, from v0.10.0, OpenBSD (pf, see OpenBSD).

What it serves

Listener Path Purpose
LISTEN_ADDR (:8443) POST /api/v1/enroll verify, choose the tenant, allocate an address, add the peer, return the tunnel configuration
GET /api/v1/tenants the tenants the caller may connect to
POST /api/v1/heartbeat renew the device’s lease
POST /api/v1/deregister remove the peer
GET /healthz liveness
GET /.well-known/claimward-configuration public discovery document, unauthenticated (since v0.13.0), see the protocol
GET /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg the server’s logo, unauthenticated, only when SERVER_LOGO_FILE is set (since v0.14.0), see the protocol
/admin/ admin API and WebUI, when the admin-token credential exists
GRPC_ADDR (:8444) claimward.routes.v1.RouteService/Watch streams the tenant’s routes and their updates
METRICS_ADDR (no default: off unless set) GET /metrics Prometheus metrics, on a listener of their own, never on LISTEN_ADDR

The API requests carry Authorization: Bearer <token>: a GitHub access token, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token, depending on the provider they name in the Claimward-Provider header (since v0.14.0, see Identity providers). See the enrollment protocol for the payloads.

With TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY both listeners use TLS. Without them the HTTP API is plain (terminate TLS at a proxy), and so is the RouteService, which the clients then refuse except on loopback: devices connect, but get no live route updates.

Configuration

Settings are in the environment. Secrets are not: since v0.6.0 they are files in a credentials directory, see Credentials below.

Variable Required Default Notes
PROVIDERS_FILE ✅ — JSON file listing the identity providers (since v0.14.0, breaking), see Identity providers. It replaces AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID: the server refuses to start while one of them is set
GITHUB_API_URL https://api.github.com the API the tenants’ named members are resolved against; set for GitHub Enterprise. Each github provider has its own api_url in the providers file
SERVER_LOGO_FILE — an SVG logo published in the discovery document and at /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg (since v0.14.0); at most 64 KiB, validated at start (no script, no external reference): an invalid file refuses to start
GOAUTHN_PEER_LIST_INTERVAL 30s how often the list of registered keys is fetched
GOAUTHN_SSF false also poll the provider’s Shared Signals stream, so that a disabling is acted on at once; the gateway’s client must be an SSF receiver there
GOAUTHN_SSF_INTERVAL 5s how often the SSF stream is polled
WG_ENDPOINT ✅ — public host:port of the gateway, advertised to clients
CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY ✅ — the directory that holds the secret files, see Credentials
WG_INTERFACE wg0 interface to manage
WG_DRYRUN false log peer operations instead of applying them (local development)
VPN_CIDR 10.80.0.0/24 IPv4 address pool; its first host is the gateway’s
PUSH_ROUTES VPN_CIDR CSV routes of the default tenant
DNS — CSV DNS servers of the default tenant
TENANTS_FILE — JSON file of tenants loaded at start, with their access policy
KEEPALIVE 25 persistent keepalive advertised to clients (seconds)
LEASE_TTL 24h how long an enrollment lasts without a heartbeat
TUNNEL_MTU derived MTU of the WireGuard interface, 1280 to 9000, advertised as mtu; anything else refuses to start. Unset: the uplink MTU minus 80, at most 1420, at least 1280. The same atomic inet claimward table also clamps the MSS of every TCP SYN crossing the interface (forwarded both ways, and input for the gateway itself) to this MTU minus 40 (IPv4) or 60 (IPv6)
LISTEN_ADDR :8443 HTTP listen address
GRPC_ADDR :8444 RouteService listen address; Watch streams are re-authorised every 15 s and end when the identity is no longer allowed
METRICS_ADDR — (off) separate listener for /metrics, served only when set (since v0.9.0 there is no default port: the old 127.0.0.1:9090 clashed with Prometheus); never on LISTEN_ADDR. It names every tenant: keep it on loopback or a private network
MAX_DEVICES_PER_SUBJECT 5 devices one identity may enroll
SERVER_NAME — display name published in the discovery document (since v0.13.0); at most 100 characters, no control characters; unset, none is published
SERVER_EXCLUSIVE false published in the discovery document (since v0.13.0): this server refuses to share the machine with other Claimward tunnels; clients refuse to connect it alongside others, and refuse others while it is connected. true or false, anything else refuses to start
GRPC_ENDPOINT — host:port of the RouteService advertised to clients; empty, they do not watch
TLS_CERT / TLS_KEY — HTTPS, and TLS on the RouteService
DEBUG — any value: debug logging (one line per request)

Credentials

Every secret is a file in the directory named by CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, never an environment variable: an environment is copied into every child process and every crash dump. systemd sets the variable for LoadCredential= and LoadCredentialEncrypted=; on the other platforms you set it yourself. The file names are fixed, and one trailing newline is trimmed.

File Required Content
wg-private-key always the gateway’s base64 private key
admin-token no bearer of the admin API and WebUI; without the file they are disabled
provider-<id>-gateway-secret a go-authn provider the gateway client’s secret (was goauthn-gateway-secret, before v0.14.0)
provider-<id>-secret each github provider the client secret of that provider’s GitHub OAuth app (see github_client_id; was github-client-secret, before v0.14.0)
github-token when any tenant has members bearer for GET /users/{login} (see Tenants)

A missing required file stops the start and names the file. Before reading, the server checks each file through its open descriptor (O_NOFOLLOW, then fstat) and refuses a symbolic link, anything but a regular file, a file readable by group or other, a file not owned by the server’s uid, an empty file and one over 64 KiB. One exception since v0.7.1: a file owned by uid 0 with mode exactly 0440 is accepted when its group is the server’s gid or one of its supplementary groups (what a Kubernetes Secret volume with fsGroup produces). A second one since v0.9.0, for systemd with DynamicUser=yes: systemd leaves the file root:root, mode 0400, plus a read-only POSIX ACL entry for the service’s uid (src/core/exec-credential.c:338-361, src/shared/acl-util.c:448-494), so stat shows 0440. The server reads system.posix_acl_access from the open descriptor and accepts exactly user:: (no write or execute), user:<its uid>:r--, group::---, mask::r--, other::---; any other named user or group, any write or execute bit, or a malformed or oversized value is refused. The error gives the fix.

Platform CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY Owner and mode
systemd set by LoadCredentialEncrypted= with DynamicUser=yes (as shipped): root-owned with a read-only ACL for the service’s uid, accepted; with a fixed User= on a filesystem without ACLs: the service user, 0400. Private tmpfs
Docker Swarm /run/secrets, set by hand mode: 0400 on the secret
Docker Compose /run/secrets, set by hand the host file’s: chown and chmod 0400 it, and set user: to match
Podman /run/secrets, set by hand --secret ...,mode=0400 (Quadlet: Secret=...,mode=0400)
Kubernetes the Secret volume’s mount path, set by hand defaultMode: 0440 and fsGroup: the files are root:<fsGroup>, accepted by the group rule above, so the pod runs as a non-root uid with every capability dropped but NET_ADMIN. add: [NET_ADMIN] alone does not give a non-root uid the capability (no ambient set): the image’s binary needs setcap cap_net_admin=+ep (per capabilities(7), not measured on a cluster)
s6 (no systemd) /run/sdcreds/claimward-server, set by sdcreds s6-run the service user, 0400, in a private tmpfs (see s6)
otherwise any directory chmod 0400, owned by the service user

Ready-made units for systemd, Compose, Podman, Kubernetes and s6 are in the repository’s deploy/ directory, with the systemd-creds encrypt steps. Hosts without systemd get the same directory from go-authn/sdcreds (see s6); the server does not depend on it.

The organisation check of the github provider does not use github-token: it runs with the person’s token, so a private membership is visible only if that token carries read:org. The credential is optional while only organisations are used.

Migrating from v0.5.0 (breaking). ADMIN_TOKEN, WG_PRIVATE_KEY, WG_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_SECRET_FILE are no longer read, and the server refuses to start while one of them is set, naming the file to create. Put each value in its file (admin-token, wg-private-key, goauthn-gateway-secret), unset the variable and set CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY. A tenant with members now also needs github-token.

Identity providers

Since v0.14.0 the server accepts several identity providers at once. They are listed in the JSON file named by PROVIDERS_FILE (unknown fields are refused, 1 MiB at most):

{"providers":[
 {"id":"campus","kind":"oidc","name":"Campus","oidc_issuer":"https://idp.example.org","oidc_client_id":"claimward"},
 {"id":"hub","kind":"github","name":"GitHub","github_client_id":"Iv1.0123456789abcdef","allowed_orgs":["my-org"]}
]}
kind Fields besides id, kind, name Secret file
github github_client_id, api_url (GitHub Enterprise), allowed_orgs provider-<id>-secret
oidc oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, allowed_domains none
go-authn oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, gateway_client_id provider-<id>-gateway-secret
  • github: the bearer is a GitHub OAuth access token from the device flow. The server asks GitHub (Check a token) with the provider’s secret before trusting it, so only tokens that OAuth app minted are admitted, then resolves it through the GitHub API (/user, /user/orgs) and admits an active member of one of allowed_orgs, or a named tenant member (the list is optional only when a tenant has members). No client ID, no secret file, or neither an allowlist nor named members: the server refuses to start, with no opt-out.
  • oidc: the bearer is an OIDC ID token, verified against the issuer with the audience oidc_client_id and the optional allowed_domains (the token’s email must be verified).
  • go-authn: the bearer is an access token (at+jwt) from a go-authn/bridge provider, and the device’s key must be registered there by the same person. The server reads the provider’s signed list of registered keys (go-authn/wireguard) and drops from wg0 a key the provider takes back. At most one provider is of this kind.

The request names its provider. Every API call carries the header Claimward-Provider: <id> (gRPC: the metadata claimward-provider), and its token is judged by that provider alone: a token of provider A is refused when the request names B. No header is 401 missing_provider, an id the server does not list is 401 unknown_provider. The discovery document lists the providers (never a secret), so a client needs only the server’s URL.

One identity per issuer and sub. The identity is issuer#sub for oidc and go-authn, and github:<id> for github: the same sub at two issuers is two people, and the second cannot take over the first’s device.

Tenants. A tenant gains a providers field, and its groups are written <provider id>:<group>. With several providers, a tenant that uses domains or idps must name providers, or the server fails closed.

Upgrading to v0.14.0 (breaking). AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID are no longer read, and the server refuses to start while one is set, naming the file that replaces it. Write the providers file, rename github-client-secret to provider-<id>-secret and goauthn-gateway-secret to provider-<id>-gateway-secret, write tenant groups as <provider id>:<group>, and expect a new subject for every person (issuer#sub, github:<id>), so devices enrol again. Use client v0.9.0 or later: older clients do not send the header.

See Identity providers for each flow end to end.

Enrollment rules

  • A key belongs to whoever enrolled it. Enrolling a key another identity holds is refused (409 key_taken): a public key is public, and taking one over would give the power to deregister its owner’s device.
  • The same key enrolled again by its owner keeps its address and gets a new lease.
  • The peer’s only allowed IP is the device’s /32, so devices cannot use each other’s addresses.
  • The tenant is the one the caller asked for, if they are a member, or their only one. See Tenants.

How it programs the gateway

The server uses wgctrl to add and remove peers on an existing interface, and checks at start-up that the interface exists. The interface itself (its private key and listen port) is left to wg-quick or systemd-networkd at boot, which keeps the privileged interface setup out of the long-running service.

OpenBSD (pf)

From v0.10.0 the server also runs on OpenBSD, where it enforces the access policy with pf instead of nftables. It talks to the kernel directly through the /dev/pf ioctls; it never runs pfctl, and there is no pfctl fallback.

  • Supported releases: OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0. They share one struct pf_rule layout, which the server checks against the running release. On any other release the server refuses to start rather than risk encoding a rule wrongly.

  • You own pf.conf. The server never edits the main ruleset. Add one line to /etc/pf.conf and keep pf enabled:

    anchor "claimward"

    The server loads the policy into that anchor. At start it reads the main ruleset back and verifies that it calls anchor "claimward".

  • It refuses to start when /dev/pf cannot be opened read-write (it must start as root), when pf is disabled, when the main ruleset does not call the anchor (the policy would be loaded and filter nothing), and when pf.conf has set skip on for the WireGuard interface (wg0, wg*), because pf would then never see the peers’ traffic.

  • Same policy as on Linux. Default deny on traffic arriving on WG_INTERFACE; only IPv4 is allowed, and IPv6 across the tunnel is dropped. The MSS clamp (TUNNEL_MTU) covers both families, as a match ... scrub (max-mss N) rule.

  • Atomic and fail closed. The anchor and its tables are replaced in one pf transaction, then read back and compared with what was meant to be loaded. If that fails, deny-all is loaded. The anchor stays in place when the process exits. Table names carry a per-load generation suffix, so that the short window between the table commit and the rule commit can never apply one tenant’s rules to another tenant’s peers.

  • Privilege separation (from v0.11.0). The pf promise of pledge(2) lets a process issue only twelve of the DIOC* ioctls (sys/kern/kern_pledge.c, pledge_ioctl), and the server also needs DIOCRINADEFINE, DIOCXROLLBACK, DIOCGETRULES, DIOCGETRULE, DIOCXEND and DIOCRGETADDRS; any other ioctl would kill the process. So the root parent, which drives /dev/pf, is not pledged. The unprivileged _claimward child, which holds the secrets and serves the network, is restricted with unveil(2) and pledge(2) before it serves (see below).

  • WireGuard peers (from v0.11.0). Before v0.11.0 an enrolment on OpenBSD failed when it added the peer to wg(4) (issue #79). The server now writes peers with the SIOCSWG and SIOCGWG ioctls of sys/net/if_wg.h and reads them back with its own decoder. Verified in real OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0 amd64 virtual machines: the structure layout matches the C compiler’s, and add, replace, remove and sweep work on a real wg(4) interface. OpenBSD on arm64 is only cross-compiled, not run on a kernel.

Deploying on OpenBSD (rc.d)

From v0.10.1 the repository ships deploy/openbsd/: an rc.d(8) script, an environment.example, a hostname.wg0.example and a pf.conf.example.

  • Two processes (from v0.11.0). The WireGuard peer configuration of wg(4) is behind suser(9) (sys/net/if_wg.c), and /dev/pf is guarded only by its device node, which is root-only: pfopen (sys/net/pf_ioctl.c) checks nothing else. OpenBSD has no privileged group that would let an unprivileged user do either, so the script starts the daemon as root (daemon_user="root") and the daemon splits in two. The parent (root) adds and removes peers, sets the tunnel MTU and loads the pf anchor; it reads no credential, serves no network and unveil(2)s only /dev/pf. The child, run as the _claimward user, holds the secrets, the TLS and gRPC listeners, the identity provider and the tenant policy, and is restricted with unveil(2) and pledge(2) (stdio rpath inet dns) before it serves. If it cannot drop privileges, the server does not start. The child asks the parent through a socketpair, and the parent refuses anything outside the address pool (VPN_CIDR).
  • The _claimward user must exist and the ports must be above 1024 (the defaults 8443 and 8444 are); to serve on 443, redirect it with a pf rdr-to.
  • Secrets are files in /etc/claimward/credentials, a 0700 directory owned by _claimward, with each file 0400 and owned by _claimward (install(1)). The script sets CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY to it; no secret goes in the environment, in arguments or in a URL. The non-secret settings are in /etc/claimward/environment, which stays root’s.
  • wg0 must exist before the server starts: hostname.wg0 carries the same private key as the wg-private-key credential (mode 0640).
install -m 0555 claimward-server /usr/local/bin/claimward-server
useradd -g =uid -c claimward -d /var/empty -s /sbin/nologin -r 1..999 _claimward
install -d -m 0755 -o root -g wheel /etc/claimward
install -d -m 0700 -o _claimward -g _claimward /etc/claimward/credentials
install -m 0400 -o _claimward -g _claimward wg-private-key /etc/claimward/credentials/wg-private-key
install -m 0600 -o root -g wheel environment.example /etc/claimward/environment # then edit
install -m 0640 -o root -g wheel hostname.wg0.example /etc/hostname.wg0 # then edit
sh /etc/netstart wg0
install -m 0555 claimward_server /etc/rc.d/claimward_server
rcctl enable claimward_server
rcctl start claimward_server && rcctl check claimward_server

rcctl start reports (ok) only once the server accepts connections on LISTEN_ADDR; a daemon that exits first, for instance on a credential the _claimward account does not own, is (failed).

The log goes to syslog (/var/log/daemon). The CI runs this script in real OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0 virtual machines: rcctl start, the startup line, rcctl check, a root parent with one _claimward child, an enrolment through the child whose peer appears on wg0, and rcctl stop; then a start with a credential owned by root, and a start without the anchor in pf.conf, which must both fail.

Deploying under s6 (sdcreds)

From v0.10.2 the repository ships deploy/s6/claimward-server/ (run and finish) for hosts without systemd. sdcreds s6-run (go-authn/sdcreds v0.2.0 or later) decrypts every file of its --source directory into a private tmpfs, writes each one 0400 and owned by --user, sets CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, and starts the server as that user. A file owned by the process’s own uid with no group or other access is the first shape the loader accepts, so the loader is unchanged. Nothing secret goes in the environment, in argv or in a URL.

  • One capability, kept on purpose. The server needs CAP_NET_ADMIN (wgctrl, nftables, the interface MTU). s6-run empties every capability set of the service by default and keeps no_new_privs; the example passes --keep-cap=CAP_NET_ADMIN, so the server runs with exactly that one (CapEff 0x1000). The capability acts on the network namespace the supervision tree runs in: the host’s, unless you start s6-svscan inside one of its own (ip netns exec).
  • Names. Each file of --source is named like its credential (wg-private-key, github-token, admin-token, provider-<id>-secret, provider-<id>-gateway-secret) and encrypted with sdcreds encrypt --name=<that name>; any other name stops the start. s6-run needs root and CAP_SYS_ADMIN (it mounts).
  • Configuration that is not secret goes in /etc/claimward/env, read by the run script.
  • Containers do not need it: Compose, Podman and Kubernetes mount secrets as files already (table above).

The CI runs this directory under a real s6-svscan, in a network namespace with a real WireGuard link and nftables (not a dry run). It checks that the log holds the public key derived from the encrypted credential (and not a control key), that the server runs as the service user with CapEff 0x1000 and no_new_privs, that no secret is in its environment, that a credential file with mode 0644 is refused, and that stopping the service removes the mount.

Run locally

With WG_DRYRUN=true no WireGuard device is touched:

cat > providers.json <<'EOF'
{"providers":[{"id":"google","kind":"oidc","name":"Google","oidc_issuer":"https://accounts.google.com","oidc_client_id":"xxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com"}]}
EOF
export PROVIDERS_FILE=$PWD/providers.json
export WG_ENDPOINT=vpn.example.com:51820
export CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY=$HOME/.local/state/claimward-dev-creds
(umask 077; mkdir -p "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY"; wg genkey > "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/wg-private-key")
chmod 0400 "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/wg-private-key"
export WG_DRYRUN=true LISTEN_ADDR=:8080

go run ./cmd/claimward-server

task run:dev does the same with GitHub sign-in and an ephemeral key, and task dex runs a local Dex to sign in against (deploy/dev/).

Run behind TLS. Bearer tokens are credentials: always serve the API over HTTPS, either with TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY or behind a TLS-terminating proxy, and give the RouteService a certificate so that devices get live route updates.

item.title: Client library
item.description:
claimward-vpn-client v0.12.0 is a Go library. It ships no binary: the runnable programs are the apps’ (cmd/claimward-app and cmd/claimward-helper in each app repository). The server imports it too, for the wire types and the gRPC stubs.

There is no claimward command-line client. Earlier versions of this module had one (cmd/claimward, with login and connect); it was removed, and the library-only module is what the apps build on.

Packages

Package Purpose
pkg/protocol the wire contract (/enroll, /tenants, /heartbeat, /deregister), shared with the server
pkg/routespb generated gRPC/protobuf stubs of the RouteService, shared with the server
pkg/auth interactive sign-in behind a Provider: GitHub device flow (default), OIDC code + PKCE, or go-authn device flow, whose provider also registers the device’s key (KeyRegistrar)
pkg/oidc the OIDC authorization code + PKCE flow: discovery, loopback redirect
pkg/browser opens a URL in the default browser with absolute opener paths, so it works from GUI apps
pkg/client Enroll, Tenants, Heartbeat, Deregister against the server, and TunnelConfig to turn an EnrollResponse into a wgtun.Config
pkg/wgkey WireGuard key generation and parsing
pkg/pathmtu fits the tunnel MTU to the path: the server’s mtu (default 1420), lowered to the interface MTU towards the endpoint minus 60 (IPv4) or 80 (IPv6), never below 1280, never above the server’s value; standard library only
pkg/wgtun userspace WireGuard tunnel with wireguard-go, plus address and routes: ifconfig/route on macOS, ip on Linux, a Wintun adapter through winipcfg on Windows (with DNS and MTU); needs privileges
pkg/routeclient watches the server’s RouteService and reports route updates; TLS except to loopback
pkg/appcore the apps’ logic, shared by the three: sign-in, the tenant chosen for the session, connect and disconnect through the helper, status for the UI
pkg/appvm the apps’ view model, with no UI in it: the screen to show, what each command may do, the status poll, the events (tunnel dropped, session expired) and, since v0.12.0, each tunnel’s facts (State.Tunnel: interface, address, endpoint, allowed IPs, DNS, MTU, bytes received and sent, last handshake); each app adapts it to its own widgets
pkg/helper the privileged helper, shared by the three apps: enrolls, owns the tunnel, watches route pushes, and approves servers with the system’s consent (Server approval)
pkg/hproto, pkg/helperclient the helper’s socket protocol, and the app’s client for it: Approve, ApproveElevated, Revoke, Approved, and the typed errors *NotApprovedError and ErrApprovalDenied
pkg/macauth macOS Authorization Services for server approval: Obtain(prompt) in the app, Verify in the helper
pkg/tokenstore the session (bearer, refresh token, device private key, chosen tenant) in the OS secret store: macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI, Linux Secret Service; no plaintext fallback

Files on the device

File What
<config dir>/Claimward/config.json the app’s configuration (appcore.Config), 0600, its socket may be overridden by CLAIMWARD_HELPER_SOCKET
<config dir>/claimward/session.enc (macOS and Linux), session.dpapi (Windows) the sealed session; its key is in the Keychain (macOS) or the Secret Service (Linux), or the blob is DPAPI-protected. On Linux the blob is sealed with AES-GCM and only its key is in the Secret Service.

<config dir> is Go’s os.UserConfigDir(): ~/Library/Application Support on macOS, ~/.config on Linux, %AppData% on Windows.

This is the format of client v0.10.0 and later, which connects to several servers at once. The person types only a server URL; the name, providers, exclusivity and logo are read from the server’s /.well-known/claimward-configuration.

{
 "version": 2,
 "servers": [
 {"url": "https://vpn.example.com", "provider": "campus"},
 {"url": "https://lab.example.org"}
 ],
 "socket_path": "/var/run/claimward-helper.sock"
}
config.json key
version 2
servers[].url the server’s base URL (https://; http:// only for loopback); must be one the helper is configured for
servers[].provider optional: the id of the provider chosen from the server’s document
socket_path optional: the helper’s socket, if not the default. May be overridden by CLAIMWARD_HELPER_SOCKET, the only variable left

A file of v0.9.0 or earlier (server_url, provider, github_client_id, oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, and the CLAIMWARD_SERVER, CLAIMWARD_AUTH_PROVIDER, CLAIMWARD_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, CLAIMWARD_OIDC_* variables) is migrated once on first load. An exclusive server is refused while any other is connected, and any other is refused while an exclusive one is; the refusal names the blocking server. Since v0.11.0 every platform holds one tunnel per server, each on its own deterministic interface (below).

Since v0.11.0 the helper’s servers is optional (the administrator’s pre-approval) and a server the person adds is trusted only once the system has consented: see Server approval. The helper’s helper.json gains approvals, the file of approved servers.

Use in your own tooling 

ctx := context.Background()

// 1. Sign in. GitHub is the default provider (device flow).
provider, err := auth.New(auth.Config{Provider: "github", GitHubClientID: "Iv1.0123456789abcdef"})
if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
}
tok, err := provider.Login(ctx, func(p auth.DevicePrompt) {
 fmt.Printf("visit %s and enter code %s\n", p.VerificationURI, p.UserCode)
})
if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
}

// 2. A key pair, and with go-authn the PUBLIC key registered first: the
// token for the server is the one RegisterKey returns.
keys, err := wgkey.Generate()
if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
}
if reg, ok := provider.(auth.KeyRegistrar); ok {
 if tok, err = reg.RegisterKey(ctx, tok, keys.Public.String(), "laptop"); err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
}

// 3. Enroll; "" lets the server use the person's only tenant.
c := client.New("https://vpn.example.com")
resp, err := c.Enroll(ctx, tok.Value, keys.Public,
 protocol.DeviceInfo{Name: "laptop", OS: "linux", Platform: "my-tool"}, "")
if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
}

// 4. The tunnel (needs privileges), and optionally live routes.
cfg, err := client.TunnelConfig(resp, keys.Private)
if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
}
tun, err := wgtun.Up(cfg)
if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
}
defer tun.Close()
if resp.GRPCEndpoint != "" {
 go routeclient.Watch(ctx, resp.GRPCEndpoint, tok.Value, keys.Public.String(),
 func(u routeclient.Update) { _ = tun.UpdateRoutes(u.AllowedIPs) })
}

A long-lived client renews its lease with c.Heartbeat before resp.LeaseExpiresAt, and removes its peer with c.Deregister when it is done.

Platform notes

  • DNS. The server’s DNS servers are applied on Windows only; on macOS and Linux they are carried in the protocol but pkg/wgtun does not apply them yet.
  • Route pushes replace the allowed IPs and the routes; DNS changes in a push are not applied.
  • Interface names. One interface per server, named from the server’s URL by wgtun.InterfaceName: macOS utunN (numbered by the kernel), Linux cw- and ten hex digits of the URL’s SHA-256 (13 bytes, within the 15 of IFNAMSIZ), Windows Claimward <host> <6 hex>. Reconnecting replaces the interface; a leftover of that name is removed first, and a Linux TUN device goes with its process, so a crashed helper leaves none.
  • Windows. The device is a Wintun adapter, one per server (see above): wintun.dll (from https://www.wintun.net, signed by WireGuard LLC) must sit beside the executable that calls wgtun.Up, which the Windows app’s packaging takes care of. Address, routes, DNS and MTU are set through winipcfg (the IP Helper API, pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0).
  • Session store. The platform’s secret store: the macOS login Keychain (holding an AES-GCM key; the session is sealed in session.enc), Windows DPAPI (session.dpapi), and on Linux a sealed session.enc too, whose AES-GCM key is kept in the Secret Service through secret-tool. Since v0.5.0 there is no plaintext fallback and CLAIMWARD_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_SESSION has no effect: with no usable store, saving the session fails and sign-in fails with an error naming what is missing (on Linux, install and unlock a Secret Service provider such as gnome-keyring or KeePassXC, and secret-tool). A legacy session.json is read once, moved into the store and deleted, or deleted if the store refuses it. Tests of other packages use tokenstore.UseMemory().

item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Claimward separates a control plane, the server, from the data plane, the WireGuard tunnel between a device and the gateway. Authentication is delegated to your identity provider: Claimward never sees a password.

On a device, an unprivileged app signs the person in and keeps the session; a privileged helper (root, or SYSTEM on Windows) enrolls with the server and owns the tunnel. The app never talks to the server itself.

End-to-end enrollment flow 

 ┌──────────┐ 1. sign-in: GitHub device flow, OIDC code + PKCE, ┌──────────┐
 │ app │ or go-authn device flow (+ key registration) │ IdP │
 │ (as you) │◀─────────────────── bearer token ──────────────────│ │
 └────┬─────┘ └──────────┘
 │ 2. socket: connect {server_url, bearer, private key, tenant}
 ▼
 ┌──────────┐ 3. POST /api/v1/enroll ┌─────────────────────────┐
 │ helper │ Authorization: Bearer <token> │ claimward-vpn-server │
 │ (root) │ {public_key, device, tenant} ───▶ │ verify the bearer │
 │ │ │ choose the tenant │
 │ │ ◀─── 4. {assigned_ip, │ allocate an address │
 │ │ server_public_key, endpoint, │ wgctrl: add the peer │
 │ │ allowed_ips, dns, │ (AllowedIPs = ip/32) │
 │ │ grpc_endpoint, keepalive, └───────────┬─────────────┘
 │ │ lease_expires_at} │ RouteService
 │ │ ◀═════════════ 6. gRPC Watch (TLS) ═══════════════╛ (live routes)
 │ │
 │ │ 5. wireguard-go: utunN / Wintun "Claimward", address, routes
 └────┬─────┘
 ╚═══════════════════ WireGuard tunnel ════════════════════▶ private network
  1. The app signs the person in with the configured provider: GitHub by default (OAuth device flow), any OpenID Connect issuer (authorization code with PKCE, in the browser), or a go-authn provider (device flow). The bearer it gets is a GitHub access token, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token. With go-authn, the device’s public key is first registered at the provider, and the bearer is the token that registration returns.
  2. The app generates the device’s WireGuard key pair at the first sign-in and keeps it in its encrypted session file (session.enc, whose key is in the Keychain or the Secret Service; session.dpapi on Windows) until the person signs out, so the device keeps its public key across connections (and its address while it is enrolled). To connect, it hands the helper the server URL, the bearer, the private key and the tenant chosen for the session, over the helper’s socket.
  3. The helper checks that the server is one its own configuration names, then calls POST /api/v1/enroll with the device’s public key and the bearer.
  4. The server verifies the bearer (a GitHub API call, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token whose subject must own the key), applies any organisation or email-domain allowlist, picks the tenant, allocates a VPN address and programs the gateway (wgctrl) with a peer whose only allowed IP is that /32. It answers with the tunnel parameters: the address, its own public key, the endpoint, the tenant’s routes and DNS servers, the keepalive, the RouteService endpoint and the lease’s end.
  5. The helper brings up a userspace tunnel with wireguard-go, gives the interface its address and installs the routes.
  6. When the server advertises a RouteService (GRPC_ENDPOINT), the helper watches it over gRPC: route changes made to the tenant reach the device without enrolling again.

Leases

Each enrollment carries a lease of LEASE_TTL (24 hours by default). A background reaper on the server removes, every minute, the peers whose lease has ended, so a lost or revoked device falls off the gateway on its own. With go-authn a lease never outlives the key’s registration at the provider.

The server renews a lease on POST /api/v1/heartbeat, and removes a peer at once on POST /api/v1/deregister.

From claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1, that is from the app releases that carry it (the macOS, Linux and Windows apps from v0.2.0), the helper keeps the lease itself while the tunnel is up. It renews at half of what the lease has left, never sooner than 30 seconds nor later than 10 minutes, and acts on the answer:

The server answers The helper
a renewed lease renews again at half of it
404 not_enrolled: it forgot the device (the lease ran out, or the server restarted) enrolls again with the same key and tenant, and brings the tunnel up from that answer; if that fails too, takes the tunnel down
403 (not_a_member, key_not_registered): access withdrawn takes the tunnel down, and reports why (last_error)
401, a 5xx, or nothing retries within a minute, sooner than the lease ends

The helper renews with the last bearer it was given. That is enough for a GitHub token, not for a go-authn access token, which expires in minutes and which only the app can refresh. So while the app runs, pkg/appcore hands the helper a fresh bearer (the helper’s renew action) at 40% of what the lease has left (at most 8 minutes apart), before the helper’s own renewal is due. An app restarted under a running tunnel starts doing so at its first status poll.

Disconnect (the helper’s down) deregisters the peer, giving its address back at once. A helper that is stopping (its service manager stops it, or the machine shuts down) takes the tunnel down without deregistering, so a helper restarted finds the lease still there, and a stopped machine’s lease runs out on the server.

The v0.1.0 apps are built on earlier client versions, which do none of this: they renew a lease only by connecting again, and leave the peer on the gateway after Disconnect until its lease ends.

Trust boundaries

  • The server is the only component that talks to the identity provider to verify a sign-in, and the only one with rights to change the gateway’s peers.
  • On the device, the helper is the only privileged process. Anything that can reach its socket can ask it to act, so it acts within its own configuration: it enrolls only with the servers that configuration names and takes no tunnel configuration from a request. See Privileged helper.
  • The app runs as the person. It holds the session (bearer token and device key) in an encrypted file, never in clear on disk: sealed with a key kept in the macOS Keychain or the Linux Secret Service, or with Windows DPAPI. With no usable store, sign-in fails.
  • A route watch carries the bearer token, so it runs over TLS except to a loopback address.
  • The wire contract lives in one place, claimward-vpn-client/pkg/protocol and pkg/routespb, imported by both the clients and the server.

item.title: Tenants
item.description:
A tenant is a set of routes (allowed_ips) and DNS servers, and the rules that say who belongs to it. A person may belong to several tenants: they choose one per session, and the device connects to that one.

Membership

A person belongs to every tenant that names any of:

Field Matched against
domains the domain of a verified email address (an unverified one is a string the person typed)
groups the token’s groups claim (OIDC; go-authn: eduPerson entitlements), or the person’s GitHub organisations
idps the institution that vouched for them: go-authn’s idp, a SAML entity ID
members GitHub logins, named one by one, pinned to the account’s numeric ID (below)
A person who matches no tenant is refused (v0.5.0, breaking): 403 not_a_member on /api/v1/tenants and /api/v1/enroll, and the gRPC Watch is refused. There is no fallback tenant any more: the default tenant receives only those its own domains, groups, idps or members name. An unknown tenant ID is an error, never the default tenant’s routes.

Migrating from v0.4.x. People who used to land in default must now be named by it: give the default entry of TENANTS_FILE the domains, groups, idps or members that name them, then restart. The default tenant created from PUSH_ROUTES and DNS alone names nobody.

Named members

members lists GitHub logins, readable but renameable: a login can be released and registered by somebody else. The server therefore pins each login to the account’s numeric ID. When a tenant is loaded (TENANTS_FILE) or created or updated through the admin API, it calls GET {GITHUB_API_URL}/users/{login} (10 s timeout, 64 KiB answer cap, the account must be a User) and stores the pair in the read-only pinned field. A person is a member when their token’s subject is github:<id> for a pinned ID: a renamed account whose old login now belongs to somebody else is refused. An unresolvable login is an error: the server refuses to start, and the admin API answers 400. The admin API and WebUI show the logins; to follow a rename, edit the tenant again. Resolution is authenticated with the github-token credential (a file in CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, sent as a bearer: 5000 requests an hour on github.com). A tenant with members and no github-token stops the start; the token is never sent over plain HTTP except to a loopback address.

A named member is also admitted by the GitHub entry gate without belonging to an allowed organisation (see identity providers).

Where tenants come from

The server starts with one tenant, default, whose routes are PUSH_ROUTES (by default VPN_CIDR) and whose DNS servers are DNS. Other tenants are created, edited and deleted through the admin API and WebUI, which edit the four membership lists beside the routes. The default tenant cannot be deleted.

Tenants are kept in memory (v0.2.0): a restart of the server leaves only the default tenant, rebuilt from the environment.

Access policy

A tenant’s routes are not only advertised: the gateway enforces them. A tenant may carry a policy, a list of rules that say which destination a peer may reach, on which protocol and ports:

[{"id": "default", "policy": [
 {"cidr": "10.20.0.5/32", "proto": "tcp", "ports": [445, 88]},
 {"cidr": "10.20.0.5/32", "proto": "udp", "ports": [88]}
]}]
  • proto is tcp or udp; ports are numbers or ranges ("9000-9010"), and are required. IPv4 only.
  • The allowed_ips pushed to the clients are derived from the policy (the distinct CIDRs), so what a device routes and what the gateway lets through cannot drift apart. The route format is unchanged.
  • The gateway owns one nftables table, inet claimward, installed through netlink (Linux, CAP_NET_ADMIN), or on OpenBSD the pf anchor claimward loaded through /dev/pf (see OpenBSD). Either is replaced atomically at start and at every peer or tenant change. Traffic arriving from the WireGuard interface is denied by default, in both the forward chain and the input chain (the file server may be the gateway host itself); each peer’s address is matched against its tenant’s rules. DNS must be named in the policy like anything else.
  • Fail closed: if the ruleset cannot be installed, the server does not start, and an enrollment whose ruleset cannot be installed is refused (500 gateway_error).
  • A tenant with allowed_ips and no policy is enforced as any protocol, any port, to those CIDRs.

Tenants with a policy are loaded at start from the JSON file named by TENANTS_FILE (an array of tenants with the admin API’s fields); the admin API accepts policy too. The admin WebUI does not edit it yet.

Choosing one per session

Request What the server does
GET /api/v1/tenants lists the tenants the caller may connect to, [{"id", "name"}], for a client to offer the choice
POST /api/v1/enroll with tenant the tenant must be one of them, or 403 not_a_member
POST /api/v1/enroll without tenant the caller’s only tenant; a person in several gets 409 tenant_required, with the list in the message, rather than being routed into a network they did not choose
POST /api/v1/heartbeat refused with 403 not_a_member once the person is no longer in the session’s tenant
RouteService Watch streams the routes of the tenant the device enrolled into, found by the device’s key, which must be the caller’s

In the apps (pkg/appcore):

  • Tenants asks the server, through the helper, which tenants the person may join;
  • SetTenant records the choice in the session, and only a tenant the server offered; a new sign-in forgets it;
  • Connect enrolls into that tenant. A person in several who has not chosen gets ErrTenantRequired, with the tenants in the status.

A person in one tenant never chooses. The macOS app opens its window when a Connect from the menu bar is refused for want of a choice; the Linux and Windows apps show the choice in their window. The Linux app does not let the tenant change while connected.

Route updates

Editing a tenant’s routes bumps its serial and pushes the new set to every device watching that tenant over the gRPC RouteService. The helper replaces the WireGuard peer’s allowed IPs and adds or removes the matching routes, without enrolling again. Deleting a tenant ends its watches.

item.title: Operations
item.description:
TLS

The server speaks plain HTTP unless TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY are set. Bearer tokens are credentials, so always put the API behind TLS, directly or through a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, a load balancer).

The same certificate serves the gRPC RouteService. A route watch carries the bearer token, and the clients refuse a plaintext watch except on loopback: a server without TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY (for instance behind a proxy that only terminates HTTPS) enrolls devices, but they get no live route updates, and it logs a warning at start-up. Set GRPC_ENDPOINT to the host:port the devices reach the RouteService at, with a name the certificate covers.

Gateway

  • Bring up wg0 with wg-quick or systemd-networkd at boot; Claimward only manages its peers. Run the server with the rights to configure the interface and the firewall: on Linux root or CAP_NET_ADMIN (nftables); on OpenBSD root, for /dev/pf (see OpenBSD).
  • On Linux, enable net.ipv4.ip_forward, and NAT or firewall rules, if clients route beyond the VPN subnet.
  • GET /healthz is the liveness probe.

Leases

LEASE_TTL (24 hours by default) balances security and churn. The reaper removes expired peers every minute, so revoked or offline devices drop off on their own. To revoke one now, deregister its peer, or remove it with wg set wg0 peer <key> remove.

From claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1 (the apps from v0.2.0), the helper renews the lease while the tunnel is up, at half of what is left (between 30 seconds and 10 minutes), and deregisters on Disconnect. A shorter LEASE_TTL therefore costs more heartbeats, not dropped tunnels: a removal from a tenant, or a key the go-authn provider takes back, ends the tunnel at the next renewal (the server answers 403). A server that has forgotten a device (404) gets it enrolled again. See Leases.

The v0.1.0 apps renew only by connecting again, and leave the peer until its lease ends after Disconnect: with them, a device that stays connected longer than LEASE_TTL loses its tunnel when its peer is reaped.

State

The server keeps the enrolled peers, the address pool and the tenants in memory. A restart forgets them:

  • the tenants are back to default alone, from PUSH_ROUTES and DNS;
  • from server v0.2.0, the peers a previous run left on wg0 are removed at startup: every peer whose only allowed IP is a /32 inside VPN_CIDR, the shape the server gives every peer. Any other peer (configured by hand, a site-to-site link) is left alone. Kept, those peers would be nobody’s: never reaped, never checked against the provider’s list, so a person disabled before the restart would keep a working tunnel. Devices find themselves unknown at their next lease renewal and enroll again (apps built on claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1); until then their tunnel carries nothing. The helper renews at most 10 minutes apart, so after a restart a device can be cut off for up to 10 minutes. Reconnecting brings it back at once.
  • the v0.1.0 server leaves those peers on wg0: it never reaps them, and it may hand their addresses to new devices (WireGuard then routes the address to the new peer). After restarting it, flush the peers (wg-quick down wg0 && wg-quick up wg0, or wg set … remove) and have devices connect again.

For several gateways or a durable audit trail, the store, ipam and tenant packages need a database behind them.

Identity provider

Since v0.14.0 the server takes one or several providers from the JSON file named by PROVIDERS_FILE (required, 1 MiB at most). The old variables AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID are refused at start. A github provider needs a GitHub OAuth App with Device Flow enabled, its client secret in the file provider-<id>-secret, and allowed_orgs to restrict access. An oidc provider needs a native/public PKCE client, and allowed_domains restricts it. A go-authn provider uses the gateway’s own client (gateway_client_id, secret in provider-<id>-gateway-secret): the provider then decides which keys may connect, and a gateway that cannot fetch its list admits nobody new. Every request names its provider in the Claimward-Provider header (401 missing_provider, 401 unknown_provider). SERVER_LOGO_FILE publishes a logo at /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg. After a change to the file, restart the server. See Identity providers.

Admin API and WebUI

With the admin-token credential present (a file in CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, see Credentials), the server serves an embedded Svelte WebUI at /admin/ and an API under /admin/api/, guarded by Authorization: Bearer <contents of admin-token> (compared in constant time). Without the file, /admin/ answers 503. The WebUI’s files are served without authentication; it asks for the token and sends it with each call.

Method & path
GET /admin/api/overview {"tenants", "peers", "watchers"} counts
GET /admin/api/tenants every tenant
POST /admin/api/tenants create one: id (or a slug of name), name, domains, groups, idps, members (logins; pinned is read-only, 400 if a login does not resolve), allowed_ips, dns
GET /admin/api/tenants/{id} one tenant
PUT /admin/api/tenants/{id} replace its name, membership lists and routes; bumps serial and pushes the routes to its watchers
DELETE /admin/api/tenants/{id} delete it (not default); ends its watches

Serve /admin/ only where administrators reach it: the token is a static shared secret.

Metrics

GET /metrics serves Prometheus metrics, without authentication, on its own listener: METRICS_ADDR, which has no default, so there are no metrics unless you set it (never on the enrollment port). They name every tenant: keep that listener on loopback or a private network.

Metric
claimward_enrollments_total{tenant} successful enrollments
claimward_active_peers enrolled peers
claimward_tenants configured tenants
claimward_route_watchers active RouteService watches
claimward_tenant_route_serial{tenant} each tenant’s route serial
